taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes subspecies longicaudus has been proposed as a distinct species (Collins 1991) but most authors keep it as a subspecies.
fieldMarks: Legless with movable eyelids, external ear openings and a lateral groove; tail more than half of length; adults 57-107 cm.
Narrow dark stripes below the lateral groove and under the tail; young and medium-sized animals have a dark middorsal stripe or dashes.
Old adults may be brown with irregular dark-bordered crossbands; males become flecked whitish and can look salt-and-pepper.
behavior: Mostly diurnal, occasionally crepuscular or nocturnal; surface activity is triggered by warm summer rains; often seen on roads in spring.
Eats grasshoppers, crickets, katydids, beetles, spiders, snails and occasionally eggs and small vertebrates; forages on and under the ground.
Tail breaks off readily (almost 80% of adults in one study had a regrown tail); overwinters in burrows below the frost line.
habitat: Open grassland, prairie, woodland edge, oak savanna, longleaf pine flatwoods and fallow fields, often on sandy soil.
range: Eastern and central United States, from the southern end of Lake Michigan and Wisconsin south through Texas and eastward to the Atlantic coast; Wisconsin populations are disjunct. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Eastern glass lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Eastern glass lizard has no stripe on the middle of the back and no stripes below the lateral groove.

lookalikes.name: Snakes (legless look-alikes)
lookalikes.howToTell: Glass lizards have eyelids and ear openings, rigid bodies and very long tails; snakes have fixed eye coverings and no ear openings.

aliases: Western slender glass lizard (O. a. longicaudus)
Eastern slender glass lizard (O. a. attenuatus)
